They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

defender-for-cloud.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (AZ-500)
defender-for-cloud.intro: Defender for Cloud (formerly Azure Security Center + Azure Defender) is the primary security posture management and workload protection service on Azure. AZ-500 tests Secure Score interpretation, which workload protection plans to enable, regulatory compliance mapping, and the distinction between Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint.

flashcards.front: What is Secure Score and how do you raise it?
flashcards.back: Secure Score is a percentage summarizing how well your Azure environment follows security recommendations — each recommendation is worth a defined number of points. To raise it: remediate recommendations, enable MFA, apply missing OS patches, restrict public network access, enable logging. It is not a compliance score — it measures posture, not a specific standard.

flashcards.front: Defender for Cloud workload protection plans — name three and their targets.
flashcards.back: Defender for Servers: agent-based threat detection, vulnerability assessment, adaptive application controls for VMs. Defender for SQL: anomaly detection and vulnerability scans for Azure SQL / SQL Server on VMs. Defender for Containers: runtime threat detection, image scanning, and hardening for AKS and container registries. Each plan is enabled per subscription and has its own per-resource cost.

flashcards.front: Regulatory compliance in Defender for Cloud — what does it do?
flashcards.back: Maps Azure resource configurations to specific controls in frameworks such as PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, and the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark. The dashboard shows passing vs failing controls per standard. It does not certify compliance — it shows your current posture against the standard's control requirements so you know what to remediate before an audit.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (MDfC) vs Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDfE) — key distinction.
flashcards.back: MDfC is an Azure-native service that monitors cloud resource configurations, detects threats across Azure workloads, and manages security recommendations across subscriptions — cloud security posture management (CSPM) + cloud workload protection (CWPP). MDfE is an endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent installed on Windows/macOS/Linux devices that detects malware, behavioral anomalies, and provides threat hunting. MDfC can integrate MDfE data but they serve different scopes.

ai.title: Azure AI Services (AZ-900)
ai.intro: Azure AI Services (formerly Cognitive Services) provide pre-built AI capabilities accessible via REST APIs — no ML training required. AZ-900 tests which service to use for a given scenario: vision, language, speech, or decision. Azure Machine Learning Studio is tested separately as the platform for building and deploying custom ML models.

flashcards.front: Azure AI Services categories — name the four pillars and a capability from each.
flashcards.back: Vision: Computer Vision (image tagging, OCR), Custom Vision (custom image classifiers), Face API (detection, verification). Language: Azure AI Language (sentiment, NER, key phrases), Translator (text translation), LUIS (intent + entity extraction). Speech: Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech, Speaker Recognition. Decision: Personalizer (RL-based recommendations), Content Moderator, Anomaly Detector.

flashcards.front: Azure Machine Learning Studio — what are its two authoring surfaces?
flashcards.back: Designer: drag-and-drop visual pipeline for users who prefer not to write code — connect dataset, transform, and model modules to build training pipelines. Notebooks: Jupyter-compatible environment for Python/R code; integrates with Azure ML SDK. Both surfaces produce the same underlying AzureML Pipelines and compute resources; the choice is workflow preference, not capability.

flashcards.front: What are the six principles of Microsoft Responsible AI?
flashcards.back: Fairness (systems treat all people equitably), Reliability & Safety (consistent performance, safe failure modes), Privacy & Security (data protection), Inclusiveness (benefits everyone, accessible), Transparency (understandable decisions), Accountability (humans remain responsible for outcomes). The AZ-900 exam expects you to name all six and recognize which principle a given scenario violates.

flashcards.front: Azure OpenAI Service vs standard Azure AI Language — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Azure AI Language: lightweight, task-specific NLP (sentiment, key phrase, NER, translation) — fast, cheap, no prompt engineering. Azure OpenAI: access to GPT-4, GPT-3.5, DALL-E via Azure's compliant infrastructure — use when you need open-ended generation, summarization, code completion, or RAG patterns. OpenAI service requires access approval and is significantly more expensive per call.

swarm.title: Docker Swarm (DCA)
swarm.intro: Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in container orchestrator — simpler than Kubernetes, natively integrated with the Docker CLI. The DCA exam tests manager/worker topology, service definitions, overlay networks for cross-node communication, and Raft consensus for leader election.

flashcards.front: Manager node vs worker node — what does each do?
flashcards.back: Manager nodes maintain cluster state using Raft consensus, schedule tasks onto workers, and serve the Swarm API (docker service commands). Worker nodes receive task assignments from managers and run the containers. Managers can also run workloads unless `--availability=drain` excludes them. A Swarm should have an odd number of managers (1, 3, 5) — Raft needs (N/2)+1 quorum to elect a leader.

flashcards.front: What is a Swarm service vs a task?
flashcards.back: A service is the desired-state declaration: image, replicas, ports, resources (e.g., `docker service create --replicas 3 nginx`). A task is one running instance of the service assigned to a specific node — it maps to a single container. If a task fails, Swarm schedules a replacement. Services are the unit you manage; tasks are what Swarm creates automatically.

flashcards.front: Overlay network — what problem does it solve in Swarm?
flashcards.back: Containers on different nodes have different docker0 bridge IPs — they can't talk to each other natively. An overlay network creates a virtual L2 network spanning all nodes using VXLAN encapsulation. Containers attached to the same overlay network can reach each other by service name via Swarm's built-in DNS; traffic is encrypted with AES-256 when you add `--opt encrypted`.

flashcards.front: Raft consensus — how many managers can you lose before the cluster is unavailable?
flashcards.back: Raft requires a majority (quorum) of managers to be reachable. With 3 managers, quorum = 2; you can lose 1. With 5 managers, quorum = 3; you can lose 2. If quorum is lost, Swarm stops accepting cluster state changes (new service deploys fail) but existing containers keep running. Recover by restarting lost managers or force-promoting a worker.

dataflow.title: GCP Dataflow (Professional Data Engineer)
dataflow.intro: Cloud Dataflow is GCP's fully managed stream and batch processing service built on Apache Beam. The PDE exam tests Beam programming model concepts — pipelines, PCollections, transforms, windows, watermarks — and when to use Dataflow vs Dataproc vs BigQuery.

flashcards.front: What is a PCollection and a PTransform in Apache Beam?
flashcards.back: PCollection (Parallel Collection): an immutable, distributed dataset that flows through a Beam pipeline — can be bounded (batch) or unbounded (stream). PTransform: an operation applied to a PCollection to produce another PCollection — examples are `ParDo` (element-wise processing), `GroupByKey`, `Combine`, `Flatten`, and `Partition`. Pipelines are DAGs of PTransforms connected by PCollections.

flashcards.front: Fixed windows vs sliding windows vs session windows — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Fixed (tumbling) windows: non-overlapping, equal-sized time buckets — 'events from 10:00–10:05'. Sliding windows: overlapping, defined by size + slide interval — 'last 5-min average, updated every 1 min'. Session windows: activity-based, closed after a gap of inactivity — 'group events from a user session separated by > 30 s of idle'. Fixed for simple aggregations, session for user behavior.

flashcards.front: What is a watermark and why does late data matter?
flashcards.back: A watermark is Beam's estimate of how far event time has progressed — it tells the system 'we probably have all events up to T'. When the watermark passes a window's end, the window is emitted. Late data (events that arrive after the watermark) can be handled by triggers and `allowed_lateness` — you can re-fire a window when late data arrives. Ignoring late data produces incorrect aggregations in streaming pipelines.

flashcards.front: Side inputs in Dataflow — what are they for?
flashcards.back: A side input is extra data made available to a `ParDo` transform beyond the main PCollection. Used when you need to look up a value for every element — e.g., a small dimension table loaded as a side input so each event can be enriched without a join. Side inputs are broadcast to all worker shards; keep them small (< 100 MB) or performance degrades.

vertex-ai.title: Google Vertex AI (PDE / PCA)
vertex-ai.intro: Vertex AI is GCP's unified ML platform — it replaces AI Platform, AutoML, and several standalone services under one API surface. PDE and PCA exams test Feature Store for feature reuse, Model Registry for versioning, Pipelines for reproducibility, and the trade-offs between AutoML and custom training.

flashcards.front: AutoML vs custom training on Vertex AI — when do you choose each?
flashcards.back: AutoML: no ML code required — provide labeled data, Vertex trains and optimizes a model for you. Best for teams without ML expertise or for tabular/vision/NLP tasks where a proven architecture suffices. Custom training: bring your own code (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn) in a custom container — required when you need a specific architecture, preprocessing logic, or domain-specific objectives that AutoML doesn't expose.

flashcards.front: Vertex AI Feature Store — what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Feature Store is a centralized, managed repository for ML features. It solves training–serving skew (the exact same feature computation is used for both offline training and online inference), enables feature reuse across teams and models, and provides point-in-time correct lookups to avoid data leakage. Features are stored as entity–feature–timestamp tuples and can be served online (low-latency) or offline (batch).

flashcards.front: Vertex AI Model Registry vs Endpoint — what is each?
flashcards.back: Model Registry: versioned catalog of trained model artifacts — stores metadata, lineage, and performance metrics. Uploading a model here doesn't serve it. Endpoint: a deployed, load-balanced serving resource that routes prediction requests to one or more model versions. You import a model from the Registry into an Endpoint to serve traffic; a single endpoint can hold multiple model versions with traffic splits for A/B testing.

flashcards.front: Online prediction vs batch prediction — pick the right one.
flashcards.back: Online prediction: real-time, low-latency (< 200 ms) REST calls against a deployed Endpoint — use when a user or application needs an immediate answer. Batch prediction: Vertex reads a BigQuery table or GCS file, runs inference on all rows, writes results back — use for scheduled scoring of large datasets where latency is not a constraint. Batch is significantly cheaper per prediction.

security-profiles.title: Palo Alto NGFW security profiles (PCNSA)
security-profiles.intro: Security profiles in PAN-OS are attached to security policy rules to inspect allowed traffic — they do not block by access control, they inspect content. The PCNSA exam tests the six profile types, what each detects, and how WildFire integrates for unknown-threat analysis.

flashcards.front: What are the six security profile types on a Palo Alto NGFW?
flashcards.back: Antivirus: scans for known malware signatures in allowed traffic. Anti-Spyware: detects C2 callbacks, spyware downloads, DNS tunneling. Vulnerability Protection: blocks exploit traffic (buffer overflows, CVE exploits) targeting open sessions. URL Filtering: categorizes and allows/blocks web URLs by category. File Blocking: controls file transfers by type (e.g., block .exe uploads). WildFire Analysis: uploads unknown files to WildFire for sandbox detonation and signature generation.

flashcards.front: Antivirus profile vs Vulnerability Protection — what is the key distinction?
flashcards.back: Antivirus blocks known malicious file content (a PDF with embedded malware, a .exe that matches a malware signature) — protects against infected files traversing the firewall. Vulnerability Protection blocks exploit traffic aimed at a specific CVE in a running application or service (e.g., an HTTP request exploiting Apache Struts) — protects against in-flight exploitation attempts. Both use signature databases, but they target different phases of an attack.

flashcards.front: How does WildFire work in the profile pipeline?
flashcards.back: A WildFire Analysis profile intercepts unknown files (not matching any antivirus signature) and forwards them to Palo Alto's cloud sandbox for dynamic detonation. WildFire returns a verdict (benign / malicious / grayware) within 5 minutes and, if malicious, generates a new antivirus signature pushed to all firewalls globally within 5 minutes for public cloud or within 24h for WildFire private cloud. It closes the gap that signature-only AV leaves open.

flashcards.front: Where do security profiles get applied?
flashcards.back: Security profiles are attached to security policy rules — only rules that allow traffic can have profiles (you don't inspect traffic you already block). Best practice: create a 'strict' profile group (all six profile types at their recommended settings) and apply it as the default on all allow rules. Override with a more permissive group only for specific legitimate use cases like antivirus scanning of encrypted tunnels you terminate.

filesystem.title: Linux filesystem and storage (RHCSA)
filesystem.intro: RHCSA is heavy on filesystem operations: setting permissions with octal notation and special bits, configuring ACLs for fine-grained access, creating LVM logical volumes, mounting filesystems via fstab, and enforcing SELinux contexts. These are tasks performed in the live exam environment, so procedure matters as much as concepts.

flashcards.front: Octal permissions and special bits — what does 4755 mean?
flashcards.back: 4 = setuid bit (run as file owner, not caller), 7 = owner rwx, 5 = group r-x, 5 = other r-x. Special bits: setuid (4) on executables runs as owner; setgid (2) on directories makes new files inherit group; sticky bit (1) on directories prevents non-owners from deleting others' files. `chmod 4755 /usr/bin/passwd` is the classic setuid example.

flashcards.front: ACL vs standard Unix permissions — when do you need an ACL?
flashcards.back: Standard Unix permissions only allow one owner + one group + other. ACLs (set with `setfacl`, viewed with `getfacl`) let you assign specific read/write/execute to individual users or groups beyond those three. Example: you own `/data`, your group is `devs`, but you also want `alice` (not in devs) to have read access — add `setfacl -m u:alice:r /data`. The ACL mask controls the effective maximum.

flashcards.front: LVM — explain PV, VG, LV in one chain.
flashcards.back: Physical Volume (PV): a raw disk or partition initialized for LVM with `pvcreate /dev/sdb`. Volume Group (VG): a pool of PVs combined with `vgcreate vg0 /dev/sdb /dev/sdc` — treated as one large storage pool. Logical Volume (LV): a virtual partition carved from the VG with `lvcreate -L 20G -n data vg0` — formatted and mounted like a normal partition. The LV can be resized online without repartitioning.

flashcards.front: fstab entry — what are the six fields?
flashcards.back: Format: `<device> <mountpoint> <fstype> <options> <dump> <fsck-order>`. Example: `UUID=abc123 /data xfs defaults 0 2`. Field 5 (dump) is almost always 0 (ignore). Field 6 (fsck pass): 1 = root checked first, 2 = checked after root, 0 = skip. Always use UUIDs or LABEL= instead of device names (/dev/sdb) which can shift after reboot.

spl.title: Splunk SPL (Splunk Core Certified User/Power User)
spl.intro: SPL (Search Processing Language) is Splunk's query language. The Splunk Core exam tests the search pipeline, statistical commands (`stats`, `chart`, `timechart`), field extraction with `rex`, deduplication, transaction grouping, and lookup enrichment — all composable in a left-to-right pipe syntax.

flashcards.front: What is the SPL search pipeline?
flashcards.back: SPL is a sequence of commands separated by `|`. Results flow left to right: each command transforms the output of the previous. Example: `index=web status=404 | stats count by uri | sort -count | head 10`. The first segment (before the first `|`) is the search command that retrieves events from the index; subsequent pipes refine, aggregate, or format those events.

flashcards.front: stats vs chart vs timechart — what does each produce?
flashcards.back: `stats`: aggregate over all results into a flat table — `stats count, avg(bytes) by status`. `chart`: produce a table with one row per value of the BY clause and columns per OVER clause — good for cross-tabulations. `timechart`: time-bucketed aggregation with _time on the X-axis — `timechart span=1h avg(response_ms) by host`. Use timechart for trend charts in dashboards.

flashcards.front: What does `rex` do and when do you need it?
flashcards.back: `rex` extracts fields using a named capture group regex inline during search — e.g., `rex field=_raw "user=(?<username>\w+)"` creates a `username` field without modifying the source data. Use it when a field you need isn't already extracted by a field extraction (props.conf/transforms.conf). For permanent extraction, define it in transforms.conf; for ad-hoc exploration, use `rex`.

flashcards.front: transaction vs stats — when do you use transaction?
flashcards.back: `transaction` groups related events into a single event based on shared field values and/or time gaps — e.g., `transaction session_id maxspan=30m` groups all web events for the same session. It preserves raw event content and adds `duration` and `eventcount` fields. Use it when you need the full raw events; use `stats` when you only need aggregated values — `stats` is orders of magnitude faster at scale.

knowledge-objects.title: Splunk knowledge objects (Splunk Core)
knowledge-objects.intro: Knowledge objects are the building blocks of Splunk data enrichment: field aliases rename existing fields, calculated fields derive new ones, event types classify events, tags add metadata, macros define reusable search snippets, and data models power Pivot and Accelerated search. The Core exam tests what each object does and the order in which Splunk applies them.

flashcards.front: Field alias vs calculated field — what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Field alias: creates an alternate name for an existing extracted field — `clientip` aliased as `src_ip`. No data is duplicated; both names point to the same value. Calculated field: creates a brand-new field whose value is derived by an `eval` expression — `response_kb = bytes / 1024`. Calculated fields require the source field(s) to already exist; they add a derived column.

flashcards.front: Event types vs tags — how do they differ?
flashcards.back: Event type: a saved search that classifies events matching its criteria — e.g., `index=web status>=400` is the `http_errors` event type. Any event matching it gets the `eventtype=http_errors` field. Tags: user-defined labels attached to specific field=value pairs — e.g., tag the value `status=404` with the tag `not_found`. Tags and event types both enrich events; event types are search-based classification, tags are value-based labeling.

flashcards.front: Macros — what problem do they solve?
flashcards.back: Macros are saved SPL snippets (optionally with arguments) that can be referenced in any search using backtick syntax: `` `web_errors` `` expands to the full search string defined in the macro. They solve DRY violations — if your team writes the same 40-character filter in 50 searches, a macro means you change it in one place. Arguments (`macro(arg1,arg2)`) make macros reusable across different index names, timeframes, etc.

flashcards.front: Data models and CIM — what is each?
flashcards.back: Data model: a hierarchical schema that describes the expected fields and constraints for a type of data (Web, Network Traffic, Authentication) — the foundation for Pivot UI and accelerated searches. CIM (Common Information Model): Splunk's standard data model library with normalized field names across data sources — `src_ip`, `dest_ip`, `action` instead of vendor-specific names. CIM compliance means every app speaks the same field language, enabling cross-source correlation.

state.title: Terraform state (TF-003 / HashiCorp Certified)
state.intro: Terraform state is the file that maps your configuration to real-world infrastructure — without it, Terraform can't know what already exists. The exam tests local vs remote backends, state locking to prevent concurrent corruption, detecting drift between state and reality, and the `terraform state` command family for surgical state manipulation.

flashcards.front: What does the tfstate file contain and why is it sensitive?
flashcards.back: The terraform.tfstate file is a JSON record of every resource Terraform manages — it includes resource IDs, attributes, and importantly, any sensitive values (database passwords, generated private keys) that Terraform fetched to record the resource's full state. It must be treated as a secret: store it in a remote backend with encryption at rest and access controls, never commit it to Git.

flashcards.front: Remote backends — S3 vs Terraform Cloud — key differences?
flashcards.back: S3 backend: stores state in an S3 bucket; combine with DynamoDB table for state locking (the table holds a lock record during `plan`/`apply`). You manage the bucket, IAM, and encryption yourself. Terraform Cloud backend: managed remote state + built-in locking + remote execution + audit logs + Sentinel policies — everything in one service. Use S3 for AWS-centric teams who want full control; Terraform Cloud for multi-cloud or teams that want governance features.

flashcards.front: State drift — what is it and how do you detect it?
flashcards.back: Drift occurs when real infrastructure diverges from the Terraform state — someone manually changed a security group rule in the console, for example. `terraform plan` detects drift: it refreshes state by calling provider APIs, compares to the config, and shows a diff. `terraform refresh` updates state to match reality without changing infrastructure (use carefully — it can lose track of resources). The fix is usually to either import the manual change into config or let the next `apply` revert it.

flashcards.front: terraform state commands — name four and their use cases.
flashcards.back: `terraform state list` — show all resources in state. `terraform state show <resource>` — print all attributes for a specific resource. `terraform state mv <src> <dst>` — rename a resource in state without destroying/recreating it (e.g., after a refactor). `terraform state rm <resource>` — remove a resource from state so Terraform no longer manages it (the real resource is NOT deleted). These are surgical tools — always take a state backup before running mv or rm.

providers.title: Terraform providers (TF-003 / HashiCorp Certified)
providers.intro: Providers are plugins that translate Terraform resource blocks into API calls for a specific platform (AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, etc.). The exam tests the `required_providers` block, version constraint syntax, the lock file that pins exact versions for reproducibility, and how provider aliases let you manage multiple accounts or regions.

flashcards.front: required_providers block — what does it declare?
flashcards.back: Inside a `terraform {}` block, `required_providers` maps provider local names to their source address and version constraint. Example: `aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }`. The source is `<namespace>/<type>` on the Terraform Registry. Without this block, Terraform can still infer providers, but pinning is required for reproducible builds and is best practice.

flashcards.front: Version constraint operators — what does ~> mean vs >= vs = ?
flashcards.back: `= 5.2.1` — exact version only. `>= 5.0` — any version 5.0 or higher (risky, allows major version jumps). `~> 5.0` (pessimistic constraint) — allows patch/minor updates within the same minor version: `~> 5.0` means `>= 5.0, < 6.0`; `~> 5.2` means `>= 5.2, < 5.3`. Use `~> X.Y` to allow bugfix updates while avoiding breaking changes from a new minor version.

flashcards.front: What is .terraform.lock.hcl and why should it be committed?
flashcards.back: The dependency lock file records the exact provider versions and their checksums selected by the last `terraform init`. Committing it to version control ensures every team member and CI pipeline uses identical provider versions — without it, `terraform init` could silently upgrade a provider and introduce a breaking change. Run `terraform providers lock` to update it after intentionally changing a version constraint.

flashcards.front: Provider aliases — when do you need them?
flashcards.back: When you need two instances of the same provider with different configurations in one root module — e.g., managing resources in two AWS regions or two AWS accounts. Define a second `provider "aws" { alias = "west", region = "us-west-2" }` block, then reference it in a resource with `provider = aws.west`. Without aliases, all resources in a module use the default (no-alias) provider configuration.

modules.title: Terraform modules (TF-003 / HashiCorp Certified)
modules.intro: Modules are the unit of reuse in Terraform — a directory of .tf files that encapsulate a set of resources behind a clean interface of input variables and outputs. The exam tests root vs child modules, how to source a module (local path, Terraform Registry, Git), and how module versioning works.

flashcards.front: Root module vs child module — what is each?
flashcards.back: Root module: the working directory where you run `terraform apply` — its .tf files are the entry point. Child module: any module called from the root (or another module) via a `module {}` block. The root module is always exactly one directory; child modules can be local (`./modules/vpc`), from the Terraform Registry (`hashicorp/vpc/aws`), or from a Git URL. Modules nest arbitrarily but deep nesting hurts readability.

flashcards.front: What are input variables and outputs in a module?
flashcards.back: Input variables (`variable "name" {}`) are the module's public API — callers pass values in the `module` block. Outputs (`output "name" { value = ... }`) expose internal resource attributes to the calling module. A well-designed module hides all resource details behind variables and outputs: callers don't need to know whether you used an `aws_vpc` or a `module.shared_vpc` internally.

flashcards.front: Module source types — local vs registry vs Git.
flashcards.back: Local: `source = "./modules/network"` — good for project-internal modules, no versioning. Terraform Registry: `source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"` + `version = "5.1.0"` — versioned, public or private, downloadable by `terraform init`. Git: `source = "git::https://github.com/org/repo.git//modules/vpc?ref=v2.0"` — version-pinned via git tag/commit, useful for private modules without a registry. Always pin a version for registry and Git sources.

flashcards.front: How do you version a module on the Terraform Registry?
flashcards.back: Registry module versions map directly to Git tags on the source repository. To publish version 1.2.3, create and push git tag `v1.2.3`. Callers pin with `version = "1.2.3"` or `version = "~> 1.2"`. The registry reads the git tag list and exposes them as selectable versions. Private registries (Terraform Cloud / Enterprise) follow the same convention. Pre-release tags (e.g., `v2.0.0-beta`) are installable but not returned by default version selection.

terraform-cloud.title: Terraform Cloud (TF-003 / HashiCorp Certified)
terraform-cloud.intro: Terraform Cloud (HCP Terraform) is HashiCorp's managed platform for collaborative Terraform usage — remote state storage, remote plan/apply execution, VCS integration, policy enforcement, and cost estimation. The exam tests the run workflow, workspace model, and how Sentinel/OPA policies gate deployments.

flashcards.front: Remote state in Terraform Cloud vs a self-managed S3 backend — key differences?
flashcards.back: Terraform Cloud stores state with built-in encryption, versioning, and access controls tied to workspace membership — no bucket/DynamoDB setup required. It also integrates locking automatically with every run. S3 backend requires you to create the bucket, enable versioning, configure a DynamoDB lock table, set up IAM, and manage encryption separately. Terraform Cloud is more turnkey; S3 gives you full control and avoids vendor lock-in.

flashcards.front: Remote execution mode — what happens when you trigger a run?
flashcards.back: In remote execution mode, `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` run on Terraform Cloud's agents, not on your laptop. Your VCS commit triggers a speculative plan (no apply); a merge to the tracked branch triggers the full plan-then-apply workflow. Variables (API keys, etc.) are stored securely in the workspace, never on developer machines. You can require a manual approval gate between plan and apply.

flashcards.front: VCS integration — how does the run workflow operate?
flashcards.back: You connect a workspace to a VCS repo and branch. On every push, Terraform Cloud opens a speculative plan as a status check on the PR — reviewers see the exact diff before merge. When the PR merges to the target branch, Terraform Cloud triggers a confirmed run: plan, optional policy check, optional cost estimate, manual approval (if configured), then apply. The VCS is the source of truth; no one `terraform apply`s from a laptop in production.

flashcards.front: Sentinel vs OPA policies — what role do they play in Terraform Cloud?
flashcards.back: Policy-as-code enforcement gate that runs between plan and apply. Sentinel is HashiCorp's proprietary policy language, included in Terraform Cloud Plus/Enterprise. OPA (Open Policy Agent) is the open-source alternative, configurable in Terraform Cloud via policy sets. Policies inspect the plan JSON and can enforce rules like 'no S3 bucket without encryption', 'no instance type larger than t3.large in dev', 'all resources must have a cost-center tag'. Advisory policies warn; mandatory policies block apply.

wan.title: CCNP WAN technologies (ENARSI)
wan.intro: ENARSI covers advanced WAN designs. DMVPN is the dominant hub-and-spoke/spoke-to-spoke VPN technology; SD-WAN (Cisco Viptela) is its software-defined successor. The exam tests DMVPN phase behavior, how mGRE and NHRP combine to build dynamic tunnels, and the SD-WAN control-plane component roles.

flashcards.front: DMVPN phases 1, 2, 3 — what changes in each?
flashcards.back: Phase 1: all spoke-to-spoke traffic hair-pins through the hub — hub is the single mGRE anchor, spokes never communicate directly. Phase 2: spokes learn each other's real IPs via NHRP and build dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels — but summarization breaks because the hub can't summarize more-specific spoke routes. Phase 3: adds NHRP redirect — hub redirects spokes to talk directly, full summarization preserved at the hub, best of both worlds.

flashcards.front: mGRE + NHRP — how do they create a dynamic tunnel?
flashcards.back: mGRE (multipoint GRE) is a single tunnel interface on the hub that can accept tunnels from many spokes without a dedicated point-to-point config per spoke. NHRP (Next-Hop Resolution Protocol) maps each spoke's private overlay IP to its public underlay IP — it's the 'directory service' of DMVPN. When spoke A wants to reach spoke B, it queries the hub's NHRP server, gets B's public IP, and builds a direct dynamic GRE tunnel.

flashcards.front: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) — what does each control-plane component do?
flashcards.back: vManage: centralized management dashboard — all configuration, monitoring, policy push. vSmart: control-plane controller — distributes routing policies and OMP routes to all vEdge/cEdge devices. vBond: orchestration component — first point of contact for new devices, authenticates them and redirects to vSmart and vManage. vEdge/cEdge: the data-plane devices at each site that establish IPsec tunnels and forward traffic.

flashcards.front: DMVPN vs SD-WAN — when would you still choose DMVPN?
flashcards.back: DMVPN is a pure Cisco IOS feature requiring no additional licensing or cloud controllers — if your existing estate is all IOS/IOS-XE and the WAN is simple, DMVPN is operationally familiar and cost-free to add. SD-WAN is better when you need application-aware routing (prefer a direct internet path for Salesforce), dual-ISP failover with SLA measurement, zero-touch provisioning at scale, or non-Cisco WAN edges. DMVPN is the right answer for 'I have 10 branch offices and a spare IOS router'.

campus.title: CCNP Campus (ENCOR / SD-Access)
campus.intro: ENCOR covers Software-Defined Access as the Cisco campus architecture. SD-Access separates the underlay (traditional routed/switched network) from the overlay (VXLAN tunnels) with LISP as the control plane to track endpoints. Cisco DNA Center is the management plane. These concepts are tested together with questions on fabric roles and endpoint mobility.

flashcards.front: SD-Access three-layer architecture — underlay, overlay, control plane.
flashcards.back: Underlay: traditional IS-IS-routed network of campus switches providing IP connectivity between fabric nodes — fast, simple, stable. Overlay: VXLAN tunnels between fabric edge nodes carry segmented traffic (VNs map to VRFs); endpoints' traffic is encapsulated at the first fabric node they attach to. Control plane: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) on the Map Server tracks where each endpoint is and responds to lookup requests — decouples who an endpoint is (EID) from where it is (RLOC).

flashcards.front: LISP — EID vs RLOC — what is each?
flashcards.back: EID (Endpoint Identifier): the stable IP address of an endpoint — it doesn't change as the device roams the campus. RLOC (Routing Locator): the IP address of the fabric edge (border or edge node) currently hosting the endpoint — this changes when the device moves. The LISP Map Server maintains an EID-to-RLOC mapping database. When fabric node A wants to reach an EID, it queries the Map Server, gets the current RLOC, and sends VXLAN-encapsulated traffic there.

flashcards.front: VXLAN in SD-Access — why use it instead of VLAN?
flashcards.back: VLANs are scoped to a single broadcast domain and don't scale beyond a building or campus floor without complex STP management. VXLAN encapsulates L2 frames in UDP/IP packets, enabling L2 segment extension across an L3 underlay fabric without STP. The 24-bit VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier) supports 16 million segments vs VLAN's 4094 — essential for per-user/per-IoT-device micro-segmentation at campus scale.

flashcards.front: Cisco DNA Center vs traditional Campus Manager — what changed?
flashcards.back: DNA Center is intent-based: you declare a policy ('this user group gets access to these apps') and DNA Center translates it into device configuration across the fabric — no manual CLI per switch. It provides discovery, topology, assurance (real-time health scores), and automation (Day-0 through Day-N provisioning). Traditional Campus Manager required per-device configuration; DNA Center treats the entire fabric as a single managed system with a declarative API.

ise.title: Cisco ISE (CCNP Security)
ise.intro: Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) is the centralized policy engine for network access control. CCNP Security tests the 802.1X authentication flow, MAB as a fallback for non-supplicant devices, TrustSec for group-based segmentation, posture assessment to check device health before granting access, and profiling to identify device types.

flashcards.front: 802.1X: authenticator, supplicant, authentication server — define each.
flashcards.back: Supplicant: the end device (a laptop running a 802.1X client like Cisco AnyConnect or Windows native supplicant) that presents credentials. Authenticator: the network device (switch port or WLC) that enforces the policy — it starts out blocking all traffic except EAP. Authentication server: typically ISE running RADIUS — validates credentials against AD/LDAP and returns a RADIUS Accept with a VLAN/dACL authorization result.

flashcards.front: MAB — when and why is it used?
flashcards.back: MAC Authentication Bypass is the fallback for devices that don't support 802.1X (printers, IP phones, IoT sensors). The switch sends the device's MAC address as both username and password to the RADIUS server. ISE looks up the MAC in its endpoint database and assigns a policy. MAB is weaker than 802.1X (MAC addresses are spoofable) — assign MAB devices to a restricted VLAN with limited access rights.

flashcards.front: TrustSec SGT — what is it and how does it enable segmentation?
flashcards.back: Security Group Tags are 16-bit labels assigned to traffic when it enters the TrustSec domain (at the authenticating switch). SGTs propagate with the traffic (inline tagging or via SGT Exchange Protocol). Enforcement nodes use Security Group ACLs (SGACLs) to permit or deny based on source SGT + destination SGT pairs — e.g., 'employees (SGT 10) may not reach PCI servers (SGT 50)'. This gives policy-based micro-segmentation without static VLANs.

flashcards.front: Posture assessment — what does ISE check and what happens on failure?
flashcards.back: Posture assessment verifies that a device meets a health policy before granting full access: OS patch level, AV installed and up-to-date, firewall enabled, disk encryption on. The ISE posture agent (part of AnyConnect) runs these checks. Compliant → full access VLAN. Non-compliant → quarantine VLAN with internet access only (to download patches) or complete block. Periodic reassessment can revoke access if the device falls out of compliance during the session.

os.title: Windows OS fundamentals (CompTIA A+)
os.intro: CompTIA A+ Core 2 tests practical Windows knowledge: edition differences, filesystem capabilities, partition table formats, and the 32-bit vs 64-bit memory ceiling. Understanding these distinctions helps diagnose installation issues, hardware compatibility, and storage configuration questions on the exam.

flashcards.front: 32-bit Windows vs 64-bit — what is the memory address limit of each?
flashcards.back: 32-bit Windows can address a maximum of 4 GB of RAM (2^32 bytes). In practice, user applications get ~2 GB and the kernel gets ~2 GB; hardware-reserved addresses reduce usable RAM further (often ~3.2 GB visible). 64-bit Windows supports up to 128 GB (Home) or 2 TB (Pro/Enterprise) depending on edition. For any modern workstation with > 4 GB RAM, a 64-bit OS is mandatory.

flashcards.front: NTFS vs FAT32 vs exFAT — compare for exam purposes.
flashcards.back: FAT32: max file size 4 GB, max volume 8 TB, no permissions or journaling — legacy, used for USB drives that must work on old systems. NTFS: max file size 256 TB, full ACL permissions, journaling, encryption (EFS), compression — required for Windows system drives. exFAT: no 4 GB file limit, no permissions/journaling — designed for flash drives and SD cards that must work across Windows and macOS without NTFS overhead. Use exFAT for large external media, NTFS for internal drives.

flashcards.front: MBR vs GPT partition tables — key differences?
flashcards.back: MBR (Master Boot Record): max disk size 2 TB, max 4 primary partitions (or 3 primary + 1 extended with logical drives), 32-bit sector addressing. Legacy BIOS only. GPT (GUID Partition Table): supports disks > 2 TB, up to 128 partitions, 64-bit addressing, backup partition table at the end of disk, required for UEFI boot. All modern systems should use GPT; MBR is only needed for Windows XP compatibility or very old hardware.

flashcards.front: Windows editions — what separates Home, Pro, and Enterprise?
flashcards.back: Home: consumer features, no domain join, no Group Policy, no Remote Desktop host, no BitLocker (encrypted removable drives only). Pro: adds domain join, Group Policy, Remote Desktop, BitLocker, Hyper-V, up to 2 CPUs. Enterprise: adds AppLocker, DirectAccess, BranchCache, advanced Credential Guard, longer LTSC support channel — requires volume licensing. The A+ exam often tests whether a specific feature requires Pro or Enterprise.

os-tools.title: Windows diagnostic tools (CompTIA A+)
os-tools.intro: A+ Core 2 is heavily scenario-based: given a symptom, which tool do you open? The exam tests chkdsk for disk errors, sfc for corrupt system files, ipconfig for network config, msconfig/Task Manager for startup and performance, and Event Viewer for log analysis — knowing the exact flag or tab for each scenario is the difference between a right and wrong answer.

flashcards.front: chkdsk — what does it check and when must you schedule it?
flashcards.back: `chkdsk C:` checks for file system errors and bad sectors on a volume. With `/f` it fixes errors; with `/r` it locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implies /f). If the target volume is the system drive (C:), Windows cannot lock it while running; you'll be prompted to schedule it for the next restart. Always run `chkdsk /r` when a user reports random file corruption or 'not formatted' errors.

flashcards.front: sfc /scannow — what does it do that chkdsk doesn't?
flashcards.back: System File Checker (`sfc /scannow`) scans all protected Windows system files and replaces corrupted or missing ones from the Windows component store (WinSxS). chkdsk checks the file system structure (allocation tables, bad sectors); sfc checks file integrity of the OS itself. Run sfc when Windows behavior is abnormal after a failed update or malware infection. Run as Administrator; requires a reboot for most replacements.

flashcards.front: ipconfig — which flags do you use for which task?
flashcards.back: `ipconfig` — show current IP/mask/gateway for all adapters. `ipconfig /all` — adds MAC address, DHCP server, DNS servers, lease times. `ipconfig /release` + `ipconfig /renew` — release and re-request a DHCP lease (fix 169.254.x.x APIPA addresses). `ipconfig /flushdns` — clear the local DNS resolver cache (fix stale DNS records). The A+ exam tests the flags, not just the command.

flashcards.front: msconfig vs Task Manager — which to use for startup items?
flashcards.back: msconfig (System Configuration) manages boot options (Safe Boot, Selective Startup) and shows services/startup items, but in Windows 8+, startup app management was moved out of msconfig into Task Manager → Startup tab. Task Manager → Startup tab shows every app set to launch at login, its publisher, and the measured startup impact (Low/Medium/High). Disable startup apps in Task Manager; use msconfig for boot flags and service troubleshooting.

vulnerability-management.title: Vulnerability management (CompTIA CySA+)
vulnerability-management.intro: Vulnerability management is the systematic process of finding, classifying, prioritizing, and remediating security weaknesses before attackers exploit them. CySA+ tests CVSS scoring mechanics, how to prioritize a remediation backlog using risk matrices, the difference between remediation and mitigation, and how credentialed scans differ from unauthenticated ones.

flashcards.front: CVSS Base Score — what metrics feed it?
flashcards.back: Exploitability metrics: Attack Vector (Network/Adjacent/Local/Physical), Attack Complexity (Low/High), Privileges Required (None/Low/High), User Interaction (None/Required). Impact metrics: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability Impact (each None/Low/High). Scope (unchanged/changed) determines if the blast radius crosses a trust boundary. The base score combines these into a 0–10 value; temporal and environmental metrics adjust it for your context.

flashcards.front: Risk prioritization matrix — how do you sequence remediation?
flashcards.back: Plot vulnerabilities on a 2-D matrix: severity (CVSS score) on one axis, exposure/exploitability on the other. Critical + internet-exposed + known exploit (CISA KEV list) = patch immediately. High CVSS but internal-only, no public exploit = patch in the next cycle. Low severity + no network path = defer or accept. Never treat CVSS as a ranking by itself — a 9.8 score behind 3 firewalls may be lower risk than a 7.0 facing the internet.

flashcards.front: Remediation vs mitigation vs acceptance — define each.
flashcards.back: Remediation: permanently fix the vulnerability — apply the patch, rewrite the code, replace the component. Mitigation: reduce exploitability without eliminating the vulnerability — firewall rule, IPS signature, disable the vulnerable feature. Acceptance: formal risk acceptance documented and signed by the data owner when cost of fixing exceeds business impact. Compensating control is a variant of mitigation that satisfies a compliance requirement when the primary control is not feasible.

flashcards.front: Credentialed vs uncredentialed scan — what does each find?
flashcards.back: Uncredentialed (unauthenticated) scan: the scanner probes the network as an outsider — finds open ports, banner-grabbing vulnerabilities, default credentials, and externally exploitable issues. Credentialed scan: the scanner logs in (local admin / SSH key) and reads installed package versions, registry keys, patch levels, and configuration files — finds far more vulnerabilities with very few false positives. Always use credentialed scans on internal systems; uncredentialed scans model attacker perspective from outside.

operations.title: Network operations (CompTIA Network+)
operations.intro: Network+ tests operational fundamentals: how SNMP works for device monitoring, why baseline documentation matters, the change-management process that prevents accidental outages, and syslog severity levels that tell you how serious a message is. These appear in scenario questions where you're asked which tool to use or which process was skipped.

flashcards.front: SNMP — OID, MIB, community string, v2c vs v3.
flashcards.back: OID (Object Identifier): a dotted-number path in the MIB tree that uniquely identifies one piece of device data (e.g., `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` = ifInOctets). MIB (Management Information Base): the schema/dictionary that maps OIDs to human-readable names. Community string: a plain-text password used for SNMP v1/v2c authentication — typically 'public' (read) and 'private' (write); a well-known security weakness. SNMPv3 replaces community strings with proper user-based auth (MD5/SHA) and encryption (AES/DES).

flashcards.front: Why is network baseline documentation critical?
flashcards.back: A baseline records normal traffic volumes, CPU/memory levels, error rates, and routing tables — captured during a known-good period. When something goes wrong, you compare current readings to the baseline to spot the anomaly (utilization spiked 300%, a new route appeared, error rate tripled). Without a baseline, 'high CPU' is meaningless because you don't know what 'normal' was. Network+ expects you to identify baselining as a best practice before troubleshooting.

flashcards.front: Change management process — what are the key steps?
flashcards.back: Request change → assess risk and impact → obtain approval (CAB or manager) → schedule a maintenance window → implement → test and verify → document outcome → close. The exam distinguishes emergency changes (faster approval path for critical incidents) from standard changes (pre-approved, low-risk, routine). Skipping change management is the most common cause of self-inflicted outages.

flashcards.front: Syslog severity levels 0–7 — name them.
flashcards.back: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug. Lower number = more severe. Most organizations alert on 0–3 and log 0–6. Debug (7) produces enormous volume and is usually enabled only during active troubleshooting. The mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Erodes Wisdom, No Debate.

cabling.title: Physical cabling (CompTIA Network+)
cabling.intro: Network+ tests physical layer specifics: cable categories and their real-world speed/distance limits, the TIA-568-B wiring standard, PoE classes for powering devices over Ethernet, and common fault types like crosstalk and split pairs. These appear in both knowledge questions and troubleshooting scenarios.

flashcards.front: Cat6 vs Cat6a — what changes in speed and distance?
flashcards.back: Cat6: supports 1 Gbps (1000BASE-T) to 100 m and 10 Gbps (10GBASE-T) only to 55 m due to alien crosstalk. Cat6a ('augmented'): supports 10 Gbps to the full 100 m run by using a larger diameter and better shielding to control alien crosstalk. Use Cat6 for standard gigabit runs; use Cat6a for new 10G runs or when you want 10G path length flexibility.

flashcards.front: TIA-568-B pin-out — which wires go on which pins?
flashcards.back: 568-B (the most common standard): 1=white-orange, 2=orange, 3=white-green, 4=blue, 5=white-blue, 6=green, 7=white-brown, 8=brown. Pairs are 1-2 (orange), 3-6 (green), 4-5 (blue), 7-8 (brown). A crossover cable uses 568-B on one end and 568-A on the other, swapping pairs 1-2 and 3-6. Modern switches with Auto-MDIX detect and compensate for crossover automatically.

flashcards.front: PoE standards — what wattage does each provide?
flashcards.back: IEEE 802.3af (PoE): 15.4 W at the port, 12.95 W delivered to the device — covers IP phones, basic APs. 802.3at (PoE+): 30 W at port, 25.5 W delivered — PTZ cameras, dual-radio APs. 802.3bt (PoE++): Type 3 = 60 W; Type 4 = 90–100 W — high-power APs, video conferencing systems, thin clients. The powered device (PD) negotiates the class; the switch PSE must have sufficient total budget.

flashcards.front: Split pair vs crosstalk — what causes each and how do you detect them?
flashcards.back: Split pair: a wiring error where a twisted pair is broken up across two different pairs (e.g., pins 1 and 3 are paired instead of 1 and 2). The cable passes a continuity test but fails NEXT (near-end crosstalk) because the wire pairs no longer benefit from differential signaling. Crosstalk (NEXT/FEXT): electromagnetic coupling between pairs in a cable — caused by poor termination, untwisting too much at the connector, or using the wrong category cable. A cable tester with NEXT measurement catches both.

mixed-topics.title: Mixed exam topics
mixed-topics.intro: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

generative-ai.title: Generative AI and LLMs (AI-900 / AIF-C01)
generative-ai.intro: Generative AI exams test conceptual understanding, not implementation. You need to know what a foundation model is, how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds a model in fresh knowledge, the spectrum of prompt engineering techniques, why hallucination happens, and what content safety guardrails do — framed for a business or cloud-architect audience.

flashcards.front: What is a foundation model and how does it differ from a task-specific model?
flashcards.back: A foundation model (GPT-4, Llama, Claude, Titan) is pretrained on massive general-purpose datasets and can perform many tasks via prompting or fine-tuning — one model, many uses. A task-specific model (sentiment classifier, image classifier) is trained end-to-end for one narrow task and cannot generalize. Foundation models are expensive to train but cheap to reuse; task-specific models are cheaper to fine-tune but brittle.

flashcards.front: RAG — what problem does it solve and how does it work?
flashcards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation solves the knowledge cutoff problem: the LLM's training data has a fixed date and doesn't include your proprietary documents. RAG adds a retrieval step: the query is used to fetch relevant chunks from an external store (vector DB, search index), which are injected into the prompt as context before the model generates a response. The model reasons over fresh retrieved content without retraining.

flashcards.front: Zero-shot vs few-shot vs chain-of-thought prompting — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Zero-shot: give the model the task with no examples — fastest, works for well-defined instructions ('Summarize this text'). Few-shot: include 2–5 input/output examples in the prompt — guides format and style, better for classification or structured extraction. Chain-of-thought (CoT): ask the model to 'think step by step' — dramatically improves multi-step reasoning (math, logic) by making intermediate steps explicit before the final answer.

flashcards.front: Hallucination — what causes it and how do you mitigate it?
flashcards.back: Hallucination is when a generative model produces confident but factually incorrect output. Causes: the model pattern-matches from training data, filling gaps with plausible-sounding text when it lacks grounding. Mitigations: RAG (ground the model in retrieved facts), temperature lowering (less creative, more deterministic), citations (require the model to cite sources so outputs can be verified), human review for high-stakes content, fact-checking evaluation layers.

machine-learning.title: Machine learning fundamentals (AIF-C01 / AI-900)
machine-learning.intro: AI certification foundational exams test the conceptual vocabulary of ML: the three learning paradigms, the bias-variance trade-off that governs model generalization, how to correctly split data for unbiased evaluation, and how to read the basic metrics used to score classifiers and regression models.

flashcards.front: Supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning — define each.
flashcards.back: Supervised: training data has labels (input → known output); model learns to map inputs to outputs. Examples: classification, regression. Unsupervised: data has no labels; model finds structure — clustering (K-means), dimensionality reduction (PCA). Reinforcement learning: an agent takes actions in an environment and receives rewards/penalties; learns a policy by maximizing cumulative reward. Examples: game AI, robotic control, ad bidding.

flashcards.front: Overfitting vs underfitting — bias-variance trade-off.
flashcards.back: Underfitting (high bias): model is too simple — poor performance on training AND test data. Overfitting (high variance): model is too complex — memorizes training data, fails on unseen data (large gap between train accuracy and test accuracy). The trade-off: reduce bias by adding complexity; reduce variance by simplifying, regularizing, or adding more data. A model that's just right is in the middle: low training error and small train-test gap.

flashcards.front: Train / validation / test split — what is each set for?
flashcards.back: Training set: what the model learns from. Validation set: used during development to tune hyperparameters and choose between models — you iteratively check it, which leaks information. Test set: held out completely until the end, touched only once to report final performance — it gives an unbiased estimate of real-world accuracy. Common splits: 70/15/15 or 80/10/10. Never tune on the test set; doing so invalidates your accuracy claim.

flashcards.front: Precision vs recall vs F1 — when do you care about each?
flashcards.back: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of all instances the model labeled positive, how many were actually positive? Optimize when false positives are costly (spam filter that blocks important email). Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all actual positives, how many did the model find? Optimize when false negatives are costly (cancer screening missing a case). F1 = harmonic mean of precision and recall — use when you need balance between both. Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets.

ml-platform.title: Azure ML and Amazon SageMaker platforms (AI-900 / AIF-C01)
ml-platform.intro: AI-900 and AIF-C01 both test knowledge of the managed ML platforms offered by their respective clouds: Azure Machine Learning Studio for Microsoft, and Amazon SageMaker for AWS. The exam expects you to recognize which service component handles which part of the ML lifecycle — training, tuning, deployment, and monitoring.

flashcards.front: Azure ML Studio — Designer vs Notebooks vs Automated ML.
flashcards.back: Designer: drag-and-drop visual pipeline editor for code-free model building — connect data ingest, transform, train, and evaluate modules. Notebooks: Jupyter-compatible IDE integrated with the workspace — full Python/R code access, best for custom preprocessing or advanced models. Automated ML (AutoML): give it a dataset and a target column; it tries hundreds of algorithm + hyperparameter combinations and ranks results — fastest way to a baseline model without writing ML code.

flashcards.front: SageMaker Studio vs SageMaker Autopilot vs SageMaker JumpStart.
flashcards.back: Studio: the IDE — notebooks, experiments, feature store, pipelines, model registry all in one UI. Autopilot: automated ML on tabular data — you provide a CSV with a target column, Autopilot runs exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, and AutoML, and produces a deployable model with full code notebooks showing what it did. JumpStart: pre-trained foundation models and ML solutions you can fine-tune or deploy in one click — think model hub inside SageMaker.

flashcards.front: SageMaker compute targets — training instance vs inference endpoint.
flashcards.back: Training: you pick an EC2 instance type (ml.p3.2xlarge for GPU training) and it runs your training script; you pay only for training duration. Inference endpoint: a persistent HTTPS endpoint backed by one or more instances (ml.c5.xlarge for CPU inference) that serves predictions — you pay by the hour it's running. Multi-model endpoints (MME) can host thousands of models on one endpoint to save costs when models are infrequently called.

flashcards.front: Azure ML compute targets — compute instance vs compute cluster vs inference cluster.
flashcards.back: Compute instance: a single managed VM for interactive development in notebooks — always on, use for author work. Compute cluster: auto-scaling pool of VMs for training jobs — scales to zero when idle, scales out during training, cost-efficient. Inference cluster: AKS-backed cluster for real-time endpoint deployment at scale with load balancing and auto-scale. Azure Container Instance (ACI) is used for low-traffic or dev/test real-time endpoints.

nlp.title: Natural language processing services (AI-900)
nlp.intro: AI-900 tests the Azure AI Language service capabilities — not how to build NLP models but which pre-built feature to use for a given business scenario. Key capabilities include sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, key phrase extraction, language detection, and document summarization, plus when to use Azure AI Speech and Azure AI Translator.

flashcards.front: Sentiment analysis vs opinion mining — what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Sentiment analysis returns an overall document or sentence sentiment label (positive/negative/neutral/mixed) with a confidence score. Opinion mining (aspect-based sentiment) goes further: it identifies specific aspects mentioned in the text and the sentiment toward each — 'The food was great but the service was slow' returns food=positive, service=negative rather than a single mixed label.

flashcards.front: Named entity recognition (NER) vs key phrase extraction — what does each return?
flashcards.back: NER identifies and classifies specific named entities in text into predefined categories: Person, Location, Organization, DateTime, Quantity, URL, Email, IP Address. Key phrase extraction returns the most important phrases that capture the topics in a document — not classified by type. Use NER when you need to know what TYPE of entity something is; use key phrase extraction when you want to summarize document topics.

flashcards.front: Azure AI Language vs Azure AI Speech vs Azure AI Translator — pick the right service.
flashcards.back: Azure AI Language: text-in, analysis-out — sentiment, NER, key phrases, language detection, question answering (QnA), CLU (conversational language understanding). Azure AI Speech: audio-in-or-out — speech-to-text transcription, text-to-speech synthesis, speaker recognition, speech translation. Azure AI Translator: text-in, translated-text-out — translates documents and text between 100+ languages, with optional script transliteration and dictionary lookup.

flashcards.front: What is Custom Named Entity Recognition and when do you need it?
flashcards.back: The pre-built NER recognizes general entity types. Custom NER lets you train the model to recognize domain-specific entities that don't appear in the standard taxonomy — e.g., product SKUs, internal department names, regulatory clause IDs in legal documents. You provide labeled training examples and the service fine-tunes on your data. Use pre-built NER first; switch to custom only when your entity types are not covered.

pod-design.title: Kubernetes pod design (CKAD)
pod-design.intro: CKAD tests how well you can design pod specs that handle real-world requirements: multi-container collaboration patterns, init container sequencing, resource quotas that prevent noisy neighbors, and probes that give Kubernetes correct signals about pod health. These translate directly to exam tasks where you write or modify YAML under time pressure.

flashcards.front: Multi-container pod patterns — sidecar, adapter, ambassador.
flashcards.back: Sidecar: augments the main container — common uses are log shipping (fluentd reads the app log file) and service mesh proxies (Envoy). Adapter: transforms output from the main container to a standard format — e.g., converts proprietary metrics to Prometheus format. Ambassador: proxies outbound requests from the main container to an external service — handles retries, service discovery, circuit breaking. All three share network namespace and volumes within the pod.

flashcards.front: Init containers — what makes them different from regular containers?
flashcards.back: Init containers run to completion sequentially BEFORE any app containers start in the pod. They are perfect for setup tasks: waiting for a database to be ready, seeding a config file into a shared volume, running a DB migration. Each init container must succeed (exit 0); if one fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod. App containers don't start until all init containers have completed — this is the ordering guarantee regular containers don't provide.

flashcards.front: Resource requests vs limits — what does each do?
flashcards.back: Request: the minimum guaranteed CPU/memory reserved for the container on a node — the scheduler uses requests to decide if a node has enough room. Limit: the maximum the container is allowed to use — if it exceeds the CPU limit it is throttled; if it exceeds the memory limit the container is OOM-killed. Always set both: without requests, the scheduler can over-pack nodes; without limits, one misbehaving pod can starve the whole node.

flashcards.front: Liveness probe vs readiness probe — what does Kubernetes do differently for each?
flashcards.back: Liveness probe: if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container — used to detect deadlocks or frozen processes. Readiness probe: if it fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service endpoints so no traffic is routed to it — but does NOT restart it. Used to signal 'I'm not ready to serve traffic yet' (warming up cache, loading model). A pod can fail readiness but pass liveness and simply sit out of rotation until it's ready.

system-hardening.title: Kubernetes and OS security hardening (CKS)
system-hardening.intro: The CKS (Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist) exam is entirely about hardening. It tests pod-level security contexts that restrict container privileges, seccomp profiles that filter syscalls, AppArmor for mandatory access control, and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark controls for node-level hardening. Every card here maps to a direct exam task.

flashcards.front: securityContext — what do runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capabilities do?
flashcards.back: `runAsNonRoot: true` — Kubernetes refuses to start the container if the image's USER is 0 (root). `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` — the container's root filesystem is mounted read-only; prevents an attacker from writing to OS directories. `capabilities.drop: [ALL]` — drops all Linux capabilities; add back only what the container needs (e.g., `NET_BIND_SERVICE` to bind < 1024 ports). These three together significantly shrink the attack surface of a compromised container.

flashcards.front: Seccomp profiles — what do they restrict and where are they configured?
flashcards.back: Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) filters which Linux system calls a process can make. A seccomp profile specifies an allowlist or denylist of syscalls. In Kubernetes, apply it in the pod's `securityContext.seccompProfile`: `type: RuntimeDefault` applies the container runtime's default filter (good baseline); `type: Localhost` with a `localhostProfile` path applies a custom JSON profile from the node. The `Unconfined` type disables filtering entirely — avoid it in production.

flashcards.front: AppArmor in Kubernetes — how do you apply a profile to a container?
flashcards.back: AppArmor profiles are loaded on the node (check with `aa-status`). In Kubernetes (pre-1.30) you annotate the pod: `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>: localhost/<profile-name>`. From 1.30+ there is a first-class `appArmorProfile` field in the container securityContext. The profile constrains file access, network operations, and capabilities based on a whitelist. CKS expects you to apply an existing profile; writing profiles from scratch is not typically tested.

flashcards.front: CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — name three node hardening controls.
flashcards.back: (1) Disable anonymous access to the API server: `--anonymous-auth=false` on the kube-apiserver. (2) Enable audit logging: `--audit-log-path` + `--audit-policy-file` to record all API requests for forensics. (3) Restrict etcd access: etcd should only be reachable from the API server, protected by mutual TLS (`--cert-file`, `--key-file`, `--peer-cert-file`). Additional controls: rotate service account tokens, enable PodSecurity Admission, use network policies to segment namespaces.

sre.title: SRE and reliability concepts (GCP PCA)
sre.intro: Site Reliability Engineering concepts appear on the GCP PCA exam because Google invented SRE. The exam tests the SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy, how error budgets translate SLOs into actionable policies, what 'toil' means and why reducing it matters, and the stages of a CI/CD pipeline that reduce deployment risk.

flashcards.front: SLI vs SLO vs SLA — what is each?
flashcards.back: SLI (Service Level Indicator): the metric you actually measure — a real number. Example: '99.2% of homepage requests returned HTTP 200 in < 300 ms over the last 28 days'. SLO (Service Level Objective): the internal reliability target for that SLI. Example: 'SLI must be ≥ 99.9%'. SLA (Service Level Agreement): the contractual commitment to customers, typically weaker than the SLO to provide buffer. Example: 'we guarantee 99.5% availability'. SLI is the measurement; SLO is the goal; SLA is the promise.

flashcards.front: Error budget — what is it and how does it change engineering behavior?
flashcards.back: Error budget = 1 - SLO. If the SLO is 99.9% availability, the error budget is 0.1% — about 43 minutes/month of allowed downtime. While budget remains, engineering teams can deploy risky changes. When budget is nearly exhausted, the team freezes releases and focuses on reliability work. This makes reliability a concrete engineering constraint rather than an abstract goal — developers self-regulate to protect their own ability to ship.

flashcards.front: Toil — what is it in SRE vocabulary and why reduce it?
flashcards.back: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales linearly with service growth — on-call responses to known alerts, manual scaling operations, ticket-driven provisioning. SRE teams target keeping toil below 50% of work time. Toil is not the same as overhead (meetings, design docs) — toil specifically has no lasting value beyond getting through the moment. Automating toil frees time for engineering that permanently improves the system.

flashcards.front: CI/CD pipeline stages — what happens at build, test, and deploy?
flashcards.back: Build: compile code, resolve dependencies, create an artifact (container image, JAR, binary) — tagged with commit hash for traceability. Test: unit tests (fast, run every commit), integration tests (service dependencies spun up), end-to-end tests (full stack, slower). Deploy: push artifact to an environment (dev → staging → canary → production), often gated by test results and policy checks. Canary deployment releases to a small traffic percentage first; rollback is fast if error budget spikes.

messaging.title: Azure messaging services (AZ-204 / AZ-305)
messaging.intro: Azure offers three distinct messaging services with very different guarantees: Service Bus for reliable ordered enterprise messaging, Event Grid for event-driven routing, and Event Hubs for high-volume streaming. The AZ-204 exam tests which service fits a given architecture requirement — picking the wrong one is the most common scenario-question trap.

flashcards.front: Service Bus queues vs topics/subscriptions — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Queue: a single sender → single receiver FIFO channel with at-most-once or at-least-once delivery, sessions for ordered processing, and dead-letter queue for undeliverable messages. Topics/subscriptions: a single sender → multiple receivers via subscriber filters — one message fan-out to N subscribers, each with their own queue. Use queues for point-to-point work distribution; use topics when multiple independent consumers need the same message.

flashcards.front: Azure Event Grid — what makes it different from Service Bus?
flashcards.back: Event Grid is a push-based, serverless event routing service — publishers emit events, Event Grid routes them to subscribers based on event type and subject filters. It's optimized for routing discrete events (a blob was created, a VM status changed) to multiple endpoints (Functions, Logic Apps, webhooks) with at-least-once delivery and no persistence beyond ~24 hours. Use Event Grid for reactive, fan-out event notifications; use Service Bus when you need guaranteed ordering, sessions, or long-term message retention.

flashcards.front: Azure Event Hubs — what is its core primitive and what is it used for?
flashcards.back: Event Hubs uses partitions — a stream is divided into N parallel partitions, each an ordered sequence of events. Consumers read from partitions via consumer groups (multiple independent apps each read the full stream through their own group). Retention is configurable (1–90 days). Use Event Hubs for high-throughput streaming: telemetry ingestion, click-stream analytics, log aggregation feeding into Stream Analytics, Spark, or Flink. It is NOT a message queue — ordering is per-partition only, not global.

flashcards.front: Dead-letter queue (DLQ) — what sends a message there?
flashcards.back: A dead-letter queue captures messages that cannot be processed: the message exceeded its max delivery count (retried too many times), its TTL (time-to-live) expired before delivery, or a receiver explicitly dead-lettered it due to a processing error. Both Service Bus queues and topic subscriptions have DLQs. Monitor the DLQ depth in production — messages accumulating there means your processing logic has a bug or the message schema is unexpected.

api-gateway.title: Azure API Management (AZ-204 / AZ-305)
api-gateway.intro: Azure API Management (APIM) is a managed gateway layer that sits in front of backend APIs. AZ-204 tests the four policy sections (inbound, backend, outbound, on-error) that transform and govern requests, the rate-limiting and JWT-validation policies, response caching, and the developer portal for external API consumers.

flashcards.front: APIM policy sections — what runs in each of the four phases?
flashcards.back: Inbound: runs first on the request before it reaches the backend — authentication (validate-jwt), rate limiting (rate-limit-by-key), request transformation (set-header, rewrite-uri), IP filtering. Backend: controls how the gateway calls the backend — retry policy, circuit breaker, load balancing between backends. Outbound: transforms the response before returning to the caller — add/remove headers, mask sensitive fields, inject CORS headers. On-error: handles exceptions — return custom error responses, log diagnostics.

flashcards.front: rate-limit-by-key policy — how does it work?
flashcards.back: Limits the number of calls per key (subscription, IP, JWT claim) within a time window. Example: `<rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />` limits each subscriber to 100 calls per 60 seconds. Returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when exceeded. Use `quota-by-key` for soft monthly caps (reset monthly, not per second). These are the primary monetization / abuse-prevention levers in APIM.

flashcards.front: validate-jwt policy — what does it verify?
flashcards.back: Validates a Bearer JWT in the Authorization header (or a custom header/query param). Checks signature against a specified JWKS URI or symmetric key, verifies iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), and nbf (not before). Can also require specific claims to be present. On failure, returns HTTP 401 without forwarding to the backend. This centralizes auth at the gateway so individual backends don't need to implement JWT validation.

flashcards.front: APIM developer portal — what is it for?
flashcards.back: An auto-generated, customizable website where external developers discover, read documentation for, and subscribe to your APIs. It shows OpenAPI specs rendered as interactive try-it-out pages, subscription key management, and usage analytics. Consumers sign up, get an API key (subscription key), and test calls from the portal. It separates the developer onboarding experience from the API implementation — a standard requirement for public or partner APIs.

nmap.title: Nmap scanning (CompTIA PenTest+)
nmap.intro: Nmap is the standard tool for network reconnaissance in penetration testing.
