PenTest+ tests scan type selection (TCP SYN vs full connect vs UDP), host discovery options, service/version detection, OS fingerprinting, NSE script usage, and output formats for reporting — all in a scenario context where you must pick the least detectable or most informative scan for a given situation.

flashcards.front: nmap -sS vs -sT vs -sU — when do you choose each?
flashcards.back: -sS (SYN scan): sends a SYN, receives SYN-ACK (open) or RST (closed) without completing the TCP handshake — stealthy, not logged by most apps, requires root/admin. Most common choice. -sT (connect scan): completes the full 3-way handshake — doesn't need raw socket privileges, works as a normal user, but is logged by the target. Use when you lack root. -sU (UDP scan): probes UDP ports — much slower, unreliable (no ACK from open ports), but needed to discover DNS (53), SNMP (161), TFTP (69) etc.

flashcards.front: Service version detection and OS fingerprinting — which flags?
flashcards.back: -sV (version detection): sends probes to open ports and matches responses against a database of service signatures — reveals Apache 2.4.51, OpenSSH 8.2, etc. Critical for vulnerability mapping. -O (OS detection): uses TCP/IP stack behavior (TTL, window size, TCP options) to fingerprint the OS — requires at least one open and one closed port; best-effort, can be wrong. -A enables -sV + -O + -sC (default scripts) + traceroute in one flag — useful for thorough scans on limited scope.

flashcards.front: NSE scripts — what are they and how do you run them?
flashcards.back: Nmap Scripting Engine scripts extend Nmap with active checks beyond port scanning — vulnerability detection, authentication testing, enumeration. Categories: auth, brute, default, discovery, exploit, safe, vuln. `--script=default` runs all 'default' category scripts (equivalent to `-sC`). `--script=vuln` runs vulnerability checks. `--script=smb-vuln-ms17-010` runs a specific script. Scripts are Lua files in `/usr/share/nmap/scripts/`. Use with `-sV` since scripts often need service version info.

flashcards.front: Nmap output formats — which to use for reports vs parsing?
flashcards.back: -oN (normal): human-readable text, good for reading in a terminal. -oX (XML): machine-parseable, input for tools like Metasploit (`db_import`), Faraday, and custom scripts. -oG (grepable): one line per host, easy to `grep` and `awk` — older format but still useful for quick shell scripting. -oA (all): saves -oN, -oX, and -oG simultaneously with a common filename prefix — best practice on real engagements so you always have all formats.

vxlan.title: VXLAN and Cisco ACI (CCNP)
vxlan.intro: VXLAN (Virtual eXtensible LAN) is the data-plane encapsulation protocol used in virtually every modern data center fabric and SD-Access campus. Cisco ACI is the policy-driven SDN fabric built on VXLAN with APIC as the controller. CCNP tests VTEPs, VNIs, the BGP EVPN control plane, and ACI's object model of EPGs and contracts.

flashcards.front: VTEP and VNI — what are they?
flashcards.back: VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint): the device (switch, router, hypervisor vSwitch, or software) that originates and terminates VXLAN encapsulation. VTEPs encapsulate L2 Ethernet frames in UDP/IP (UDP port 4789) and send them across an L3 underlay. VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier): a 24-bit segment ID that identifies the VXLAN segment — 16 million possible VNIs vs VLAN's 4094. VNI is the VXLAN equivalent of the VLAN ID.

flashcards.front: VXLAN vs VLAN — why does VXLAN win in modern data centers?
flashcards.back: VLANs are limited to 4094 IDs, can't stretch across L3 boundaries without complex extensions (OTV), and require STP for loop prevention. VXLAN uses 24-bit VNIs (16M segments), runs over a standard L3 underlay (no STP), scales to thousands of switches, and enables VM/workload mobility across the data center without IP address changes. Multi-tenancy at scale — each tenant gets VNIs, not VLANs.

flashcards.front: BGP EVPN as the VXLAN control plane — what does it do?
flashcards.back: Without a control plane, VTEPs flood unknown unicast/broadcast/multicast (BUM) traffic to all VTEPs to learn MAC-to-VTEP mappings — inefficient at scale. BGP EVPN (RFC 7432) provides a control plane: VTEPs advertise their locally learned MAC/IP bindings as BGP EVPN routes (Type 2 routes). Remote VTEPs learn MAC-to-VTEP mappings via BGP before any data traffic, eliminating flooding. This is 'MAC routing' — applying routing discipline to L2 learning.

flashcards.front: Cisco ACI — APIC, spine, leaf, EPG, contract — how do they relate?
flashcards.back: APIC (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller): the SDN controller cluster that holds the intent-based policy model and pushes config to fabric switches. Spine: L3 backbone switches (no endpoints attach, only leaf-to-leaf connectivity). Leaf: access-layer switches where servers, VMs, and external networks connect. EPG (Endpoint Group): a logical group of endpoints (VMs, bare-metal) with identical policy requirements — replaces VLANs as the segmentation boundary. Contract: the policy that permits or denies traffic between EPGs — EPGs don't talk to each other unless an explicit contract allows it.

language.title: Azure AI Language services
language.intro: Azure AI Language (part of Azure AI Services) bundles ready-to-use NLP APIs — sentiment analysis, NER, key phrase extraction, question answering, and conversational language understanding — all behind a single REST endpoint. AZ-900 and AI-900 exams test which feature handles which task.

flashcards.front: What does sentiment analysis return?
flashcards.back: A document-level opinion score: positive, neutral, or negative, each with a confidence value 0-1. Sentence-level scores are also available. Use case: product reviews, social-media monitoring.

flashcards.front: Named Entity Recognition (NER) vs key phrase extraction?
flashcards.back: NER classifies entities into categories (Person, Location, DateTime, Organization). Key phrase extraction returns the most important nouns/noun phrases without categorising them. NER is richer; key phrases are faster for topic summarisation.

flashcards.front: Question Answering vs Conversational Language Understanding (CLU)?
flashcards.back: Question Answering extracts answers from a static knowledge base (FAQ document). CLU predicts intent and entities from a user utterance for multi-turn dialog flows. QA is lookup; CLU is intent classification.

flashcards.front: Azure AI Speech bundles which four services?
flashcards.back: Speech-to-Text (ASR), Text-to-Speech (synthesis), Speech Translation (real-time spoken translation), and Speaker Recognition (verify/identify by voice). All available via the same Speech SDK or REST endpoint.

variables.title: Terraform variables and locals
variables.intro: Terraform input variables make configurations reusable; locals simplify repeated expressions. The TF-003 exam heavily tests type constraints, validation blocks, sensitive flags, and the precedence order for variable assignment.

flashcards.front: Five ways to assign a Terraform variable (highest to lowest precedence)?
flashcards.back: -var flag > -var-file flag > *.auto.tfvars (alphabetical) > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR_name env var. Higher-precedence sources override lower ones.

flashcards.front: What does sensitive = true do on a variable?
flashcards.back: Redacts the value from CLI output and plan display. It does NOT encrypt the value in state — state still stores it in plaintext, so the backend must be secured separately.

flashcards.front: When to use locals vs variable?
flashcards.back: Use locals for computed or repeated expressions internal to a module that callers should not override (e.g. a concatenated name). Use variables for values callers should supply. Locals cannot be set from outside the module.

flashcards.front: Type constraint any vs object({ ... }) — trade-offs?
flashcards.back: object({ key = type }) enforces a specific schema with required keys and types — prefer this for safety. any disables type checking entirely and should only be used for dynamic wrapper modules where the type is intentionally unknown.

ml-fundamentals.title: Machine learning fundamentals
ml-fundamentals.intro: Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from data without explicit programming. Azure AI-900 exams test the four core ML task types, the train/validate/test split, and which Azure service handles each scenario.

flashcards.front: Four types of machine learning workloads?
flashcards.back: Regression (predict a number), Classification (predict a category), Clustering (group unlabelled data), Anomaly detection (find outliers).

flashcards.front: What is the role of a validation set?
flashcards.back: Tune hyperparameters and catch overfitting during training — separate from the test set, which is only touched once to report final accuracy.

flashcards.front: Deep learning vs classical ML — key difference?
flashcards.back: Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks that learn features automatically; classical ML requires manual feature engineering.

flashcards.front: Azure Machine Learning vs Azure AI Services?
flashcards.back: Azure ML is for training and deploying custom models; Azure AI Services are pre-built APIs (Vision, Speech, Language) — no training required.

gen-ai.title: Generative AI concepts
gen-ai.intro: Generative AI models produce new content (text, images, code) from prompts. AWS AIF-C01 tests foundational concepts: how foundation models work, prompt engineering basics, responsible AI, and key AWS AI services.

flashcards.front: What is a foundation model (FM)?
flashcards.back: A large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks via fine-tuning or prompting — e.g., Amazon Titan, Anthropic Claude.

flashcards.front: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — what and why?
flashcards.back: Pairs an FM with a knowledge base: retrieves relevant documents at query time and injects them into the prompt, reducing hallucinations on private/recent data.

flashcards.front: Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting?
flashcards.back: Zero-shot: prompt only; no examples. Few-shot: include 2-5 examples in the prompt to guide the model's output format or style.

flashcards.front: Amazon Bedrock's key differentiator?
flashcards.back: Serverless API access to multiple FMs from different providers (Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Amazon) without managing infrastructure.

analytics.title: AWS analytics services
analytics.intro: AWS offers a suite of managed analytics services covering data warehousing, stream processing, interactive querying, and BI. The Cloud Practitioner exam tests which service to use for each scenario.

flashcards.front: Amazon Redshift — primary use case?
flashcards.back: Columnar data warehouse for petabyte-scale SQL analytics on structured data; not for OLTP or real-time streaming.

flashcards.front: Amazon Kinesis vs SQS — when to choose Kinesis?
flashcards.back: Kinesis for real-time ordered streaming with multiple consumers and replay; SQS for decoupled task queues with at-least-once delivery.

flashcards.front: Amazon Athena — how does it query data?
flashcards.back: Serverless interactive SQL on data stored in S3; no infrastructure to manage, pay per query (per TB scanned).

flashcards.front: AWS Glue role in an analytics pipeline?
flashcards.back: Managed ETL service: crawls data sources to build a Data Catalog, then runs serverless Spark jobs to transform and load data.

cost-management.title: AWS cost management
cost-management.intro: AWS provides several tools to monitor, forecast, and reduce spending. The Cloud Practitioner exam asks which tool to use for billing analysis, budgets, and rightsizing recommendations.

flashcards.front: AWS Cost Explorer vs AWS Budgets?
flashcards.back: Cost Explorer: visualise and analyse past and forecasted spend. AWS Budgets: set spend/usage thresholds and receive alerts when approaching them.

flashcards.front: What does AWS Trusted Advisor's cost pillar check?
flashcards.back: Identifies idle or underutilised resources (e.g., low-CPU EC2, unattached EBS), Reserved Instance optimisation, and savings plan coverage gaps.

flashcards.front: Three ways to reduce AWS compute costs?
flashcards.back: Reserved Instances (1–3 yr commitment, up to 72% off), Savings Plans (flexible compute discount), and Spot Instances (spare capacity, up to 90% off).

flashcards.front: AWS Cost Allocation Tags — purpose?
flashcards.back: User-defined key-value pairs on resources; activate in Billing Console to break down costs by team, project, or environment in Cost Explorer.

pricing.title: Azure pricing models
pricing.intro: Azure pricing combines consumption-based, reservation, and hybrid-benefit models. The AZ-900 exam tests the difference between CapEx and OpEx and how Azure's pricing calculator and TCO calculator help estimate costs.

flashcards.front: CapEx vs OpEx in a cloud context?
flashcards.back: CapEx = upfront hardware purchase (on-premises). OpEx = pay-as-you-go subscription (cloud). Cloud shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx.

flashcards.front: Azure Reservations — how much can they save?
flashcards.back: Commit to 1- or 3-year terms for VMs, databases, or other services; save up to 72% compared to pay-as-you-go rates.

flashcards.front: Azure Hybrid Benefit?
flashcards.back: Use existing on-premises Windows Server or SQL Server licences (with Software Assurance) on Azure VMs to reduce or eliminate the licence cost.

flashcards.front: Azure Pricing Calculator vs TCO Calculator?
flashcards.back: Pricing Calculator: estimate cost of specific Azure services you plan to use. TCO Calculator: compare on-premises infrastructure cost against equivalent Azure deployment.

firepower.title: Cisco Firepower NGFW
firepower.intro: Cisco Firepower is Cisco's next-generation firewall platform combining traditional stateful inspection with application visibility, intrusion prevention (NGIPS), and advanced malware protection. CCNP Security exams test its architecture and policy model.

flashcards.front: FMC vs FDM — which is required for multi-device management?
flashcards.back: Firepower Management Center (FMC) manages multiple sensors centrally; Firepower Device Manager (FDM) is an on-box GUI for single-device management only.

flashcards.front: Firepower Access Control Policy hierarchy?
flashcards.back: Default action at the bottom; rules evaluated top-to-bottom first match wins. Each rule can allow, block, or redirect to IPS/AMP inspection.

flashcards.front: What does Snort inspect in Firepower?
flashcards.back: Snort is the inline IPS engine; it applies intrusion rules to decoded network traffic and can drop or alert on matching packets.

flashcards.front: AMP for Networks vs AMP for Endpoints?
flashcards.back: AMP for Networks: file reputation and sandboxing at the network perimeter via Firepower. AMP for Endpoints: host-level continuous monitoring and quarantine.

platform.title: Network platform fundamentals
platform.intro: Platform-level network concepts cover programmability, automation, and the software-defined layers that modern networks — and CCNP exams — build on top of traditional switching and routing.

flashcards.front: Cisco DNA Center — primary role?
flashcards.back: Intent-based networking controller for campus/branch: provisions devices, applies policies, and provides assurance analytics from a single dashboard.

flashcards.front: REST API verbs for CRUD operations?
flashcards.back: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). Responses use HTTP status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found, etc.

flashcards.front: YANG model — what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Defines a vendor-neutral data model for network device configuration and state, used with NETCONF and RESTCONF for structured automation.

flashcards.front: Northbound vs southbound API in an SDN controller?
flashcards.back: Northbound: API the controller exposes to applications (REST/gRPC). Southbound: API the controller uses to program network devices (OpenFlow, NETCONF, RESTCONF).

deployment.title: Kubernetes Deployment strategies
deployment.intro: A Kubernetes Deployment manages rolling updates and rollbacks for stateless Pods. CKAD exams test strategy types, rollout commands, and how resource limits interact with scheduling.

flashcards.front: RollingUpdate vs Recreate deployment strategy?
flashcards.back: RollingUpdate: gradually replaces old Pods with new ones (zero downtime). Recreate: terminates all old Pods before starting new ones (brief downtime).

flashcards.front: maxSurge and maxUnavailable — what do they control?
flashcards.back: maxSurge: how many extra Pods above the desired count can exist during rollout. maxUnavailable: how many Pods can be down at once. Both accept absolute numbers or percentages.

flashcards.front: Command to roll back a Deployment to the previous revision?
flashcards.back: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>  (add --to-revision=N to target a specific revision from rollout history).

flashcards.front: Liveness vs Readiness probe — difference?
flashcards.back: Liveness: kills and restarts the container if it fails. Readiness: removes the Pod from Service endpoints if it fails (does not restart).

pod-security-admission.title: Kubernetes Pod Security Admission
pod-security-admission.intro: Pod Security Admission (PSA) replaced PodSecurityPolicy in Kubernetes 1.25+. It enforces three built-in security profiles at the namespace level using labels. CKS exams test the profiles and enforcement modes.

flashcards.front: Three Pod Security Standards?
flashcards.back: Privileged (no restrictions), Baseline (prevents known privilege escalations), Restricted (strongly hardened — requires non-root, drops all capabilities, enforces seccompProfile).

flashcards.front: Three PSA enforcement modes?
flashcards.back: enforce (reject violating Pods), audit (log violations but allow), warn (display warning to the user but allow). A namespace can have different levels per mode.

flashcards.front: How to label a namespace for PSA?
flashcards.back: kubectl label namespace <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. Add --version=latest to pin the policy version evaluated.

flashcards.front: What does seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault do?
flashcards.back: Applies the container runtime's built-in seccomp filter (e.g., Docker's default), which blocks ~300+ dangerous syscalls — required by the Restricted profile.

build.title: Docker build and image layers
build.intro: Docker builds images layer by layer from a Dockerfile. Understanding the layer cache, multi-stage builds, and build context is essential for DCA exam questions on image size and build performance.

flashcards.front: What triggers a cache miss during docker build?
flashcards.back: Any change to a Dockerfile instruction or the files it COPYs invalidates that layer and all subsequent layers — order instructions from least to most frequently changed.

flashcards.front: Multi-stage build — main benefit?
flashcards.back: Compile or test in one stage using a full SDK image, then COPY only the binary/artifact into a minimal final stage — dramatically reduces final image size.

flashcards.front: docker build --no-cache — when to use?
flashcards.back: Forces a full rebuild from scratch, ignoring the layer cache. Useful when you need the latest base image or a fresh dependency fetch despite no Dockerfile changes.

flashcards.front: .dockerignore — purpose?
flashcards.back: Excludes files from the build context sent to the Docker daemon. Reduces build time and prevents accidentally baking secrets or large dev files into the image.

databases.title: GCP managed database services
databases.intro: Google Cloud provides managed databases spanning relational, NoSQL, and globally distributed models. GCP ACE exams test which service fits a given workload and the key trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Cloud SQL vs Cloud Spanner — key difference?
flashcards.back: Cloud SQL: managed MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server for regional workloads. Cloud Spanner: globally distributed, strongly consistent, horizontally scalable — no regional limit.

flashcards.front: Firestore vs Bigtable — choose by workload?
flashcards.back: Firestore: document/NoSQL for mobile and web apps with rich queries and real-time sync. Bigtable: wide-column store for high-throughput time-series or IoT data (no rich queries).

flashcards.front: Cloud Memorystore — what runtimes does it support?
flashcards.back: Managed Redis and Memcached — fully compatible with open-source clients, no patching required, used for caching and session storage.

flashcards.front: When would you choose AlloyDB over Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: AlloyDB is Google's PostgreSQL-compatible database optimised for analytical and transactional mixed workloads; faster than standard Cloud SQL for HTAP use cases.

pubsub.title: Google Cloud Pub/Sub
pubsub.intro: Pub/Sub is GCP's fully managed, serverless messaging service for asynchronous event-driven architectures. GCP PDE exams test topic/subscription model, delivery guarantees, and integration with Dataflow.

flashcards.front: Pub/Sub delivery guarantee — exactly-once or at-least-once?
flashcards.back: At-least-once by default — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once delivery is available with Dataflow streaming pipelines using the exactly-once processing mode.

flashcards.front: Pull vs Push subscription?
flashcards.back: Pull: consumer calls Pub/Sub API to fetch messages (subscriber controls rate). Push: Pub/Sub POSTs messages to a webhook URL (simpler for serverless like Cloud Run/App Engine).

flashcards.front: Pub/Sub Lite vs Pub/Sub — key trade-off?
flashcards.back: Pub/Sub Lite: zonal, lower cost, capacity pre-provisioned. Standard Pub/Sub: global, auto-scaling, no pre-provisioning — recommended unless cost is the primary concern.

flashcards.front: Message retention in Pub/Sub?
flashcards.back: Unacknowledged messages are retained up to 7 days by default (configurable to 10 minutes–7 days). Acknowledged messages are deleted.

dataproc.title: Google Cloud Dataproc
dataproc.intro: Dataproc is GCP's managed Apache Spark and Hadoop service. It lets you spin up clusters in seconds and integrates with GCS, BigQuery, and Pub/Sub. GCP PDE exams test cluster sizing, job types, and lifecycle.

flashcards.front: Dataproc vs Dataflow — when to choose Dataproc?
flashcards.back: Dataproc: lift-and-shift existing Spark/Hadoop jobs or when you need fine-grained cluster control. Dataflow: managed Apache Beam for new unified batch+streaming pipelines.

flashcards.front: Dataproc Autoscaling — what does it adjust?
flashcards.back: Horizontally scales the number of preemptible (secondary) workers based on pending YARN jobs — primary workers stay fixed to avoid data locality loss.

flashcards.front: Ephemeral vs persistent Dataproc cluster?
flashcards.back: Ephemeral: create for a job, delete when done — cheaper, no idle cost. Persistent: long-lived for interactive workloads or frequent jobs.

flashcards.front: How does Dataproc integrate with BigQuery?
flashcards.back: BigQuery connector lets Spark jobs read from / write to BigQuery tables directly without intermediate GCS staging, using the BigQuery Storage API for high throughput.

composer.title: Google Cloud Composer
composer.intro: Cloud Composer is GCP's managed Apache Airflow service for orchestrating complex workflows (DAGs). GCP PDE exams test DAG design, scheduling, task dependencies, and integration with BigQuery and Dataflow.

flashcards.front: What is a DAG in Airflow/Composer?
flashcards.back: Directed Acyclic Graph — a Python file defining tasks and their dependencies. Each task is an Operator; the DAG scheduler triggers runs based on schedule_interval.

flashcards.front: Sensor vs Operator in Airflow?
flashcards.back: Sensor: waits (polls) for an external condition (file in GCS, BigQuery table, time). Operator: performs an action (runs a query, submits a Dataproc job).

flashcards.front: Where does Composer store DAGs and logs?
flashcards.back: DAGs are synced from a GCS bucket; logs are stored in GCS and viewable in the Airflow UI. The metadata database runs on Cloud SQL (Postgres).

flashcards.front: Cloud Composer 2 vs 1 — key improvement?
flashcards.back: Composer 2 uses GKE Autopilot and auto-scales workers; Composer 1 uses standard GKE with fixed node pools. Composer 2 is recommended for new deployments.

defender.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
defender.intro: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Security Center + Azure Defender) is a Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) and Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP) for Azure, multi-cloud, and hybrid environments.

flashcards.front: CSPM vs CWPP — what does each do in Defender for Cloud?
flashcards.back: CSPM: continuously assesses security posture, assigns a Secure Score, and recommends remediations. CWPP: detects and responds to active threats on workloads (VMs, containers, DBs).

flashcards.front: Secure Score — what does it measure?
flashcards.back: A percentage representing how many of Defender's security recommendations you have implemented. Higher = better posture. Each recommendation has a point value.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint vs Defender for Cloud?
flashcards.back: Defender for Endpoint: EDR agent for individual Windows/Linux devices. Defender for Cloud: posture management and threat protection for cloud infrastructure.

flashcards.front: Defender for Cloud coverage beyond Azure?
flashcards.back: Supports AWS and GCP workloads via multicloud connectors, and on-premises servers via Azure Arc — providing a unified security view across environments.

licensing.title: Microsoft 365 licensing
licensing.intro: Microsoft 365 is sold in subscription plans that bundle productivity apps, security, and device management. MS-900 exams test which plan includes which features and the volume licensing options.

flashcards.front: Microsoft 365 Business vs Enterprise plans — key split?
flashcards.back: Business plans (Basic/Standard/Premium) are capped at 300 users. Enterprise plans (E1/E3/E5) have no user cap and include advanced compliance and security features.

flashcards.front: What does Microsoft 365 E5 add over E3?
flashcards.back: E5 adds advanced security (Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps), advanced compliance (Purview), and Power BI Pro — roughly doubles the cost of E3.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Volume Licensing vs Microsoft 365 subscription?
flashcards.back: Volume Licensing (EA, CSP) offers negotiated pricing, centralised management, and payment flexibility for large organisations; subscriptions are per-user/month via direct or partner channels.

flashcards.front: Difference between Microsoft 365 and Office 365?
flashcards.back: Office 365 is the older brand for productivity apps + cloud services. Microsoft 365 adds Windows 10/11 Enterprise licences and advanced security/compliance tools.

support.title: Microsoft support plans
support.intro: Microsoft offers tiered support plans for Microsoft 365 and Azure. MS-900 exams test response times, support scope, and what's included in each tier versus the default included support.

flashcards.front: Four Microsoft support plan tiers?
flashcards.back: Developer (dev/test only), Standard (production environments), Professional Direct (business-critical, faster SLAs), Unified (formerly Premier — full enterprise coverage).

flashcards.front: What support is included free with any Microsoft 365 subscription?
flashcards.back: 24/7 online self-help, documentation, community forums, and billing/account management support. Technical break-fix for critical issues is included but with no SLA.

flashcards.front: Professional Direct SLA for critical severity?
flashcards.back: Initial response within 1 hour for Severity A (business-critical outage) — compared to 2 hours for Standard.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Unified support advantage over lower tiers?
flashcards.back: Dedicated Customer Success Account Manager (CSAM), proactive services, on-demand assessments, and custom SLAs — effectively the former Premier Support contract.

teams.title: Microsoft Teams
teams.intro: Microsoft Teams is the hub for teamwork in Microsoft 365, combining chat, meetings, calling, and app integration. MS-900 exams test Teams architecture, guest access, compliance controls, and licensing.

flashcards.front: Teams channel vs chat — key difference?
flashcards.back: Channels are persistent, team-wide conversation threads stored in SharePoint. Chats are private 1:1 or group conversations stored in Exchange mailboxes.

flashcards.front: Guest access vs external access in Teams?
flashcards.back: Guest access: external users join a specific Team and get access to channels/files (requires an Azure AD guest account). External access: federate with another Teams tenant for chat/calls only — no team membership.

flashcards.front: Teams Direct Routing — purpose?
flashcards.back: Connect a customer-managed Session Border Controller (SBC) to Teams Phone, letting users make PSTN calls through an existing telephony provider without a Microsoft Calling Plan.

flashcards.front: Which Microsoft 365 licence is required for Teams?
flashcards.back: Teams is included in Microsoft 365 Business Basic and above, and Office 365 E1 and above. A free Teams (Essentials) tier exists with limited features and no Microsoft 365 integration.

users.title: Linux user and group management
users.intro: RHCSA exams heavily test creating, modifying, and deleting users and groups, managing passwords, and setting file permissions using standard Linux commands and /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group.

flashcards.front: Command to create a user with a specific UID and home directory?
flashcards.back: useradd -u 1050 -m -d /home/alice alice  (-m creates the home, -d sets the path, -u sets UID).

flashcards.front: Difference between usermod -aG and usermod -G?
flashcards.back: -aG appends the user to a group (keeping existing memberships). -G alone replaces all supplementary groups — omitting -a removes the user from any groups not listed.

flashcards.front: How to lock and unlock a user account?
flashcards.back: passwd -l <user> locks (prepends ! to the password hash). passwd -u <user> unlocks. usermod -L / -U does the same.

flashcards.front: /etc/passwd format?
flashcards.back: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell — 'x' means the password hash is in /etc/shadow. A UID of 0 means root privileges.

update-sets.title: ServiceNow Update Sets
update-sets.intro: Update Sets are the unit of deployment in ServiceNow, capturing configuration changes made in one instance so they can be transported and applied to another (e.g., dev → test → production).

flashcards.front: What does an Update Set capture?
flashcards.back: Configuration changes to the ServiceNow platform (scripts, UI policies, workflows, business rules, etc.) but NOT data records or instance-specific attachments.

flashcards.front: Update Set states: In Progress → Complete → workflow?
flashcards.back: Set the Update Set to Complete to prevent further changes, then retrieve it in the target instance and Preview to check for conflicts before Committing.

flashcards.front: What happens during Preview in the target instance?
flashcards.back: ServiceNow compares the incoming Update Set against the target's current state and flags conflicts or missing records so you can resolve them before commit.

flashcards.front: Batch Update Set — what is it?
flashcards.back: A parent container grouping multiple Update Sets so they can be transported, previewed, and committed together in the correct order.

workspaces.title: Terraform workspaces
workspaces.intro: Terraform workspaces let you manage multiple independent state files within the same configuration directory, useful for environment isolation (dev/staging/prod) without duplicating code.

flashcards.front: Commands to create and switch workspaces?
flashcards.back: terraform workspace new <name> creates and switches. terraform workspace select <name> switches to an existing one. terraform workspace list shows all workspaces.

flashcards.front: Default workspace — can it be deleted?
flashcards.back: No — the 'default' workspace always exists and cannot be deleted. It maps to the root terraform.tfstate file.

flashcards.front: How to reference the current workspace name in configuration?
flashcards.back: Use the built-in terraform.workspace variable, e.g. resource name prefix = "${terraform.workspace}-" to tag resources per environment.

flashcards.front: Workspace state storage in remote backends?
flashcards.back: In S3: state files are stored as <prefix>/<workspace>/terraform.tfstate. In Terraform Cloud, each workspace has its own isolated state, runs, and variables.

tokens.title: HashiCorp Vault tokens
tokens.intro: Tokens are the core authentication mechanism in Vault — every authenticated client uses a token to make API calls. Vault token types, TTLs, and policies determine what a client can do.

flashcards.front: Root token — when and why to use it?
flashcards.back: Generated during 'vault operator init'; has unlimited access. Should be revoked immediately after bootstrapping policies — never used for day-to-day operations.

flashcards.front: Service token vs batch token?
flashcards.back: Service token: stored in Vault, supports renewal, can create child tokens. Batch token: lightweight, encrypted, not stored — cheaper for high-throughput use cases but cannot be renewed or looked up.

flashcards.front: Token TTL vs Max TTL?
flashcards.back: TTL: how long until the token expires unless renewed. Max TTL: the absolute ceiling a token's lifetime can be extended to — renewal cannot push past it.

flashcards.front: vault token create -orphan flag?
flashcards.back: Creates a token without a parent; revocation of the creator's token does not cascade to this token. Useful for long-lived service accounts.

secrets-engines.title: Vault secrets engines
secrets-engines.intro: Secrets engines are the plugins that store, generate, or encrypt secrets in Vault. Each engine is mounted at a path and has its own API. Vault Associate/Professional exams test the major engine types and their use cases.

flashcards.front: KV v1 vs KV v2 secrets engine?
flashcards.back: KV v1: simple key-value, no versioning. KV v2: stores up to N versions of each secret; you can recover deleted secrets and compare versions.

flashcards.front: Dynamic secrets — why prefer over static?
flashcards.back: Vault generates short-lived credentials on demand (e.g., AWS IAM keys, database passwords) that auto-expire, reducing the blast radius of a leaked credential.

flashcards.front: Transit secrets engine — what does it do?
flashcards.back: Encryption-as-a-service: Vault encrypts/decrypts data without storing it. Applications send plaintext, receive ciphertext — the key never leaves Vault.

flashcards.front: PKI secrets engine — core capability?
flashcards.back: Acts as an internal Certificate Authority: issues X.509 certificates with configurable TTLs on demand, enabling automated short-lived TLS certs for services.

operator.title: Vault operator commands
operator.intro: The vault operator subcommands manage Vault's lifecycle — initialising a new cluster, unsealing after a restart, and taking snapshots. These are tested on Vault Associate exams.

flashcards.front: vault operator init — what does it output?
flashcards.back: Unseal keys (5 by default) and the initial root token. These are shown only once — store securely. The number of keys and required threshold are configurable.

flashcards.front: Shamir secret sharing in Vault unseal?
flashcards.back: The master key is split into N shares; a threshold (default 3 of 5) must be provided to reconstruct it and unseal Vault. No single person needs the full key.

flashcards.front: vault operator unseal vs auto unseal?
flashcards.back: Manual unseal: operators enter shares at the CLI (one per command). Auto unseal: Vault uses an external KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS) to decrypt the master key automatically on restart.

flashcards.front: vault operator raft snapshot save — purpose?
flashcards.back: Creates a point-in-time backup of the integrated Raft storage backend to a file. Use for disaster recovery; restore with vault operator raft snapshot restore.

dataverse.title: Microsoft Dataverse
dataverse.intro: Dataverse is the data platform underneath the Power Platform — a managed, relational store with built-in security, business logic, and a uniform Web API. PL-400 leans on it heavily: most Power Apps, plug-ins, and automations read and write Dataverse.

flashcards.front: What is a Dataverse table (formerly entity)?
flashcards.back: A table is a typed set of rows with columns, relationships, keys, and its own security. Standard tables (Account, Contact) ship with the platform; custom tables are added per solution. Each table exposes an OData/Web API endpoint automatically.

flashcards.front: How do you query Dataverse from code?
flashcards.back: Use the Web API — an OData v4 REST endpoint at /api/data/v9.x. GET with $select/$filter/$expand for reads, POST/PATCH/DELETE for writes. The SDK (IOrganizationService) wraps the same operations for plug-ins and server-side code.

flashcards.front: How is access controlled in Dataverse?
flashcards.back: Security roles grant privileges (create/read/write/delete/append) at access levels (user, business unit, parent-child, organization). Rows are owned by a user or team; business units scope visibility. This is row- and column-level security, not just table-level.

flashcards.front: Business rules vs plug-ins for logic?
flashcards.back: Business rules are no-code, run on the form and server for simple validation/defaults. Plug-ins are .NET code on the event pipeline for complex or cross-table logic. Prefer the lightest tool that meets the requirement — business rules first, plug-ins when you need real code.

plug-ins.title: Dataverse plug-ins
plug-ins.intro: A plug-in is custom .NET code registered against the Dataverse event pipeline — it runs when a row is created, updated, deleted, or another message fires. Plug-ins are the core server-side extensibility model tested on PL-400.

flashcards.front: What are the stages of the event pipeline?
flashcards.back: Pre-validation (outside the transaction), pre-operation (in transaction, before the main operation), and post-operation (in transaction, after). Pre stages can change input values; post stages react to the committed result. Choosing the right stage is a common exam point.

flashcards.front: Synchronous vs asynchronous plug-in registration?
flashcards.back: Synchronous runs inline and can block/roll back the operation — use it when the user must see the effect immediately or you must veto the change. Asynchronous runs later via the system job queue — use it for slow or non-critical work so the user isn't kept waiting.

flashcards.front: What is sandbox (isolation) mode?
flashcards.back: Plug-ins run in a partial-trust sandbox: no file system, no most native calls, and only outbound HTTP/HTTPS allowed. It's required for cloud and enforces security and tenant isolation. Design plug-ins to stay within these limits.

flashcards.front: How do you pass data into a plug-in?
flashcards.back: The execution context carries InputParameters (the Target entity/reference), pre- and post-images (snapshots of the row before/after), shared variables, and the user context. Register only the images and attributes you need to keep performance up.

power-apps.title: Power Apps: canvas, model-driven, and PCF
power-apps.intro: Power Apps is the app layer of the Power Platform. PL-400 expects you to know when to use a canvas app vs a model-driven app, and how to extend either with code components (PCF).

flashcards.front: Canvas app vs model-driven app?
flashcards.back: Canvas apps give pixel-level control over the UI and can connect to many data sources — best for task-focused, tailored experiences. Model-driven apps are generated from the Dataverse data model and security — best for complex, data-centric line-of-business apps where consistency matters more than custom layout.

flashcards.front: What is the Power Apps Component Framework (PCF)?
flashcards.back: PCF lets you build reusable code components (controls) in TypeScript/HTML that plug into canvas and model-driven apps, replacing or augmenting standard fields and grids. Use it when no out-of-the-box control meets the UX requirement.

flashcards.front: How do canvas apps talk to data?
flashcards.back: Through connectors. Dataverse is the native, most capable connector; others reach SQL, SharePoint, or any REST API via custom connectors. Delegation matters: push filtering/sorting to the source so you don't hit the local record cap on large datasets.

flashcards.front: What is a custom connector?
flashcards.back: A wrapper around a REST API (described by an OpenAPI/Swagger definition) that makes its operations available to Power Apps and Power Automate. It handles auth (API key, OAuth2) and surfaces actions as first-class steps — the standard way to integrate an external system.

solutions.title: Power Platform solutions and ALM
solutions.intro: Solutions are how you package, version, and move Power Platform components (tables, apps, flows, plug-ins) between environments. Application Lifecycle Management (ALM) on PL-400 is about doing that reliably from dev to test to production.

flashcards.front: Managed vs unmanaged solutions?
flashcards.back: Unmanaged is the editable, source form you build in your dev environment — components can be changed and the solution itself isn't a deployment boundary. Managed is the locked, deployable artifact you import into test/production; it can be cleanly upgraded or uninstalled. Develop unmanaged, ship managed.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple environments?
flashcards.back: Separate dev, test, and production environments isolate change: you build in dev, validate in test, and release to production by importing the managed solution. Never edit components directly in production — it breaks the ALM chain and can't be cleanly upgraded.

flashcards.front: How do you automate solution deployment?
flashcards.back: Use the Power Platform Build Tools (or Power Platform CLI 'pac') in a pipeline to export the unmanaged solution from dev, build a managed version, and import it to the next environment. Pipelines in Power Platform also provide a managed, low-code path for the same export/import flow.

flashcards.front: What are environment variables and connection references for?
flashcards.back: They externalise per-environment values (URLs, IDs) and connections so the same managed solution works in dev, test, and prod without hard-coded settings. You set their values at or after import — a key practice for clean, repeatable deployments.
